newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: DBS Bank reports stronger growth.
newsitem.headline: DBS Bank reports stronger growth.

text.p: The Development Bank of Singapore Ltd (DBS) said on Wednesday the group's net profits grew 13 percent to Singapore $358.29 million in the first half of the year to June 30, 1997.
Company officials said the group saw stronger growth at the bank level, which achieved an 18-percent rise in net profit to S$316.99 million.
The group's net interest income rose 23.2 percent to S$1.35 billion while group earnings per share rose to S$1.03 from S$0.92.
DBS also declared an interim dividend of nine cents compared to eight cents last year, the bank's first dividend increase in more than 10 years.
The last time DBS raised dividend rate was in 1981, when it was increased to 16 percent from 15 percent.
DBS senior vice president of finance & tax, Susan Ho, said the bank achieved double digit growth in all loan categories.

While the average loans to total asset ratio rose to 59.1 percent in the first half of 1997 from 42.0 percent in 1992, its interbank assets to total asset ratio fell to 28.1 percent from 44.2 percent during the same period.
The bank said it did not expect a major change in domestic loan growth in the second half.
A S$52.4 million provision was made in the first half of 1997 comprising general and specific provisions.
"The bulk of the provision was general provisions, set aside due to expanded loan portfolio. Specific provisions were minor. None for Thailand," said group president Ng Kee Choe.
Profits in the first half of 1997 were particularly dampened by two units, DBS Finance and NDC Merchant.

"DBS Finance saw a double digit, low teens drop in profit because profit was lower due to thinning margins and expanded loan base which requires higher general provisions," Ng said. "But we are expecting positive growth for the whole year."
In contrast, its securities trading arm DBS Securities saw a double digit growth in net profit.
Ng said the group was unscathed by the recent turmoil of South East Asian currencies.
"As a regional bank, we participate in the regional market. We make some and lost some. Overall, we were unscathed," Ng said.
